931.quote_or_event: “Just as an impassioned fish which is eager to swallow the bait, has its body transfixed by a hook.”
931.explanation: In the lecture on the causes of carelessness, the man who is passionately attached to tastes is compared to a fish that, greedy for the bait, is pierced by the hook hidden inside it.
931.tie_back: Valluvar warns that even gambling's winnings are like the bait a fish swallows with the iron hook inside; the Uttarādhyayana uses the same image of the baited hook for the pleasure that hides its own ruin.
931.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.63 (the comparison line of the verses on taste, 32.61–73) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
931._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Jacobi gives this line in a bracketed summary of the repeated verses); the bait-and-hook image matches the Kural almost exactly, but in the sūtra it describes craving for tastes, not gambling.

932.quote_or_event: “As a man for the sake of one Kâkinî (risks and) loses a thousand (Kârshâpaṇas), or as the king lost his kingdom (and life) by eating a mango-fruit which he was strictly forbidden (by his physician)”
932.explanation: Mahāvīra compares the fool who trades lasting goods for petty pleasures to a man who loses a thousand coins for the sake of a single tiny one.
932.tie_back: Valluvar says gamblers gain one and lose a hundred; the Uttarādhyayana's man who stakes and loses a thousand coins for one kākiṇī expresses the same ruinous arithmetic.
932.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
932._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the gain-one-lose-many image is nearly one-to-one (Jacobi's '(risks and)' even suggests a wager), though in the sūtra it is a parable about human versus divine pleasures; the same verse is used for Kural 831.

933.quote_or_event: “After a man has done acts which cause the death of living beings, his pleasure-seeking relations take possession of his wealth, whilst the doer of the acts must suffer for them.”
933.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that the wealth a person gathers by sinful acts passes into other hands, while he alone bears the karmic consequences.
933.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who keeps calling out stakes on the rolling dice will see his wealth and income go and fall to others; the Jain text likewise shows wealth slipping to others while the doer is left with the loss.
933._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the idea of wealth passing to others, but the cause in the sūtra is harmful action in general, not gambling, and the 'others' are relatives, not enemies.

934.quote_or_event: “After having enjoyed pleasant seats, beds, carriages, riches, and pleasures, after having squandered his wealth which he had so much trouble in gaining, and after having committed many sins, he will, under the burden of his Karman, and believing only in the visible world, be grieved in the hour of death like the ram at the arrival of a guest.”
934.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana describes the pleasure-seeker who squanders hard-earned wealth and piles up sins, only to face grief and the weight of his karma at death.
934.tie_back: Valluvar says nothing impoverishes like gambling, which brings many miseries and destroys good standing; the Jain verse likewise shows indulgence squandering hard-won wealth and ending in misery.
934.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.8–9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
934._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it captures wealth squandered through indulgence and the resulting grief, but it does not name gambling or loss of renown, so it is a next-best match.

935.quote_or_event: “He should not learn to play chess, he should not speak anything forbidden by the Law; a wise man should abstain from fights and quarrels. Shoes, an umbrella, dice, chowries, working for another, helping each other: from all this a wise man should abstain.”
935.explanation: Among the things a wise monk must give up, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga lists learning board games (aṣṭāpada) and handling dice.
935.tie_back: Valluvar says those who prided themselves on the dice, the gaming hall and their skill of hand ended with nothing; the Sūtrakṛtāṅga tells the wise to give up the dice and the gaming board altogether.
935._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it explicitly names dice and a board game (Jacobi notes 'chess' may mean any game on a chequered board), but it is a monastic rule with no account of gamblers ruined, so this is a reasonable but partial match.

936.quote_or_event: “Then when death comes at last, the fool trembles in fear; he dies the 'death against one's will,' (having lost his chance) like a gambler vanquished by Kali.”
936.explanation: Mahāvīra compares the fool who dies unprepared to a gambler beaten by Kali, the losing throw of the dice, who has thrown away his chance.
936.tie_back: Valluvar calls gambling a goddess of misfortune that swallows its victims and leaves them in want and sorrow; the Uttarādhyayana likewise uses the gambler overcome by Kali, the throw of ill luck, as its image of utter defeat.
936.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
936._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the gambler overpowered by Kali suits the image of being swallowed by misfortune, but Jainism has no goddess of misfortune like the Kural's Mugaḍi, and the verse is about the fool's death, not gambling as such.

937.quote_or_event: “Those endowed with excellent knowledge live many nayutas of years; so great a loss suffer the fools in a life of less than a hundred years!”
937.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana laments how much fools throw away when they spend their brief human life on passing pleasures.
937.tie_back: Valluvar says time passed in the gaming hall destroys inherited wealth and good character; the Jain verse likewise grieves over the great loss that comes from wasting a short human life on trifles.
937.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
937._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares only the general theme of a life wasted on pleasure, and says nothing of the gaming hall, ancestral wealth or character, so this is a weak next-best match.

938.quote_or_event: “When he is not satisfied with those 'colours,' and his craving for them grows stronger and stronger, he will become discontented, and unhappy by dint of his discontent; misled by greed he will take another's property. When he is overcome by violent desire, takes another's property, and is not satisfied with those 'colours' and their possession, then his deceit and falsehood increase on account of his greed; yet he will not get rid of his misery.”
938.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces the chain by which unchecked craving leads to discontent, then to taking others' property, then to growing deceit and falsehood, and still to misery; the preceding verse adds that the passionate man torments living beings.
938.tie_back: Valluvar lists what gambling does: it ruins wealth, drives a person to lying, kills compassion and leaves him in misery. The Jain verses trace the same chain of craving, lying and lasting misery.
938.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.29–30 (cf. 32.27) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
938._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the sequence of craving, falsehood and misery closely parallels the Kural's chain, but the subject is attachment to sense objects, not gambling.

939.quote_or_event: “He will be born among men where there is wealth, beauty, glory, fame, long life, and eminent happiness.”
939.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana says the one who has renounced pleasure will be reborn where wealth, glory, fame and happiness are found.
939.tie_back: Valluvar says that clothing, wealth, food, renown and learning never come to one who takes up gambling; the Jain verse gives the reverse case, in which a similar list of goods comes to the one who has given up pleasure.
939.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
939._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the list of worldly goods is a mirror image of the Kural's list, but it describes rebirth as a reward for renunciation, not goods lost through gambling, so the match is indirect.

940.quote_or_event: “Those will reap pains who, in thoughts, words, or acts, are attached to their body, to colours, and to forms.”
940.explanation: In the lecture on the false ascetic, Mahāvīra teaches that attachment to the body is itself a source of suffering, and in Jain thought this attachment keeps the soul (jīva) bound in saṃsāra.
940.tie_back: Valluvar ends by saying the soul loves the body all the more the more it suffers, as the gambler loves the game the more he loses; the Jain verse reverses the direction, teaching that attachment to the body is what produces the pain.
940.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
940._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the Kural's link between the soul's attachment to the body and suffering, but it does not contain the gambling comparison or the paradox of love growing with pain.
